pageCache.pageTitle: Summer: Get Active — Mazahirul Uloom London
pageCache.text:
Summer: Get Active
Long days and lighter timetables are a gift — and a chance to build habits that last. A few simple, joyful ways for our students to stay active, healthy and balanced over the summer break.
Summer arrives like an open door. The timetable loosens, the evenings stretch out, and for a few weeks the days are genuinely the students' own. It is a gift — and like any gift, what matters is what we do with it.
We say to our families every year: rest is good, and screens have their place, but a summer spent entirely indoors is a summer half-lived. The body was made to move, and a young person who stays active over the break comes back in September sharper, calmer and readier to learn.
Why movement matters
Physical activity is not only about fitness. For young people it shapes mood, sleep, focus and confidence. A brisk walk clears the head before it ever touches the heart rate. And there is a tradition in our faith of valuing strength and vitality: "The strong believer is more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though there is good in both."
A summer habit, kept for six weeks, has a way of becoming a year-round one.
Simple ways to stay active
None of this needs a gym membership or a packed schedule. The best summer activity is the kind a family will actually keep up:
Keeping the balance
A good summer holds a few things together: rest and activity, freedom and routine, play and worship. We encourage students to keep a light anchor in their day — a portion of Qur'an, the prayers on time, a little reading — so that the break refreshes them without unmooring them.
Stay active, stay balanced, and come back to us in September ready to grow. We will be glad to see you.

pageCache.pageTitle: Why We Memorise: The Heart of the Hifz Programme — Mazahirul Uloom London
pageCache.text:
There is a particular quiet that settles over a Hifz classroom in the first hour of the morning. It is not the silence of an empty room, but the low, layered murmur of a dozen students reciting under their breath — each at their own page, each holding a few more verses than they held the day before.
People often ask how a child can hold the entire Qur’an in memory. The honest answer is that memorisation is the smallest part of what is happening. What we are really teaching is attention: the capacity to sit with one thing, return to it daily, and let it change you slowly.
A discipline, not a sprint
Our students do not memorise in a rush. The Hifz+ programme runs alongside the full secondary curriculum, not instead of it. A pupil might revise a page of Qur’an in the morning, sit a science lesson before break, and return to consolidation in the afternoon.
This rhythm matters. It teaches three habits that serve students long after school:
A child who has learned to return to the same page, morning after morning, has learned something no exam can measure.
Memory and meaning together
We are careful never to treat Hifz as recitation drained of meaning. Alongside memorisation, students study tajwīd — the rules of pronunciation — and spend time with the meanings of what they carry. The goal is not a recording but a reader: someone for whom the words are alive.
For families considering the programme, the most common worry is academic. Will memorisation crowd out everything else? In our experience the opposite is true. The students who give an hour each morning to focused revision tend to bring that same steadiness to their GCSE subjects. The discipline transfers.
If you would like to understand how Hifz sits within the wider timetable, our Hifz Programme page sets out the structure, and the school office is always glad to talk it through.
What we hope they keep
Not every student who begins will complete the full memorisation, and that is part of the design — there is no shame in the attempt, and every verse held is a gift kept. What we hope each child keeps, whatever page they reach, is the habit of returning: to the text, to the discipline, and to the quiet that taught them how to pay attention.

A holistic education rooted in tarbiya
Mazahirul Uloom London is an independent Islamic secondary school in the heart of East London, combining academic ambition with the nurturing of moral and spiritual character.
Building a strong foundation for a stronger future
Our school is dedicated to fostering academic excellence and nurturing students with strong moral character, rooted in Islamic values and holistic tarbiya. We aim to shape well-rounded individuals who excel academically, uphold ethical principles, and contribute positively to their communities.
Tarbiya, an Arabic term, refers to the holistic process of nurturing a person’s moral and spiritual growth. It sits at the centre of everything we do — guiding how we teach, how we care for our students, and the community we build together.
What sets us apart
A balanced curriculum that integrates academic rigour with Islamic teachings and values.
A focus on tarbiya, promoting respect, discipline, empathy, and accountability in daily life.
Experienced and caring teachers who inspire both intellectual growth and spiritual development.
A vibrant learning environment enriched with extracurricular activities, including Hifz classes, Islamic studies, and character-building programmes.
Faith and knowledge,
character and care —
a foundation for life.
We want our children to thrive and find excellence
By instilling motivation and cultivating a love for learning today, we pave the way for a future rich with possibilities and endless achievements.
Our ambition is simple: that every child who joins us leaves with the knowledge, character, and confidence to succeed in this world and the Hereafter.
Building bridges
By instilling motivation and cultivating a love for learning today, we pave the way for a future rich with possibilities and endless achievements.
Increasing engagement
We provide a safe and nurturing environment that encourages exploration and discovery, ensuring that our students are engaged and excited to learn.
Reinventing the classroom
Our classrooms are designed to be interactive and engaging, fostering creativity and critical thinking in our students.
School life
At Mazahirul Uloom, we believe that school is more than just a place to learn. It is a community where students can grow, make friends, and create lasting memories.
Our uniform
Our uniform is a symbol of pride and unity. It instils a sense of belonging and identity in our students, fostering a strong school spirit and a sense of community.
A caring place to be
As an independent Islamic secondary school, Mazahirul Uloom London is subject to inspection by Ofsted. Inspectors have described the school as a caring place to be — a community where students are known, valued, and supported.
We are committed to safeguarding, high standards, and the welfare of every child. Our full policies are published for families and the wider community to read.
